ALL MODULES · RAPID RECALL

⚡ Master Cheat Sheet

Read this first. It gives the minimum decision logic needed to distinguish the major AWS services across Modules 1–8.

☁️ Module 1: Cloud Concepts Overview

Cloud computing = on-demand delivery + via the internet + pay-as-you-go.
IaaS/PaaS/SaaS = how much you manage; Cloud/Hybrid/On-premises = where it runs.
Six advantages: CapEx→variable expense, economies of scale, stop guessing capacity, speed/agility, stop maintaining data centers, go global in minutes.
AWS access: Console = click, CLI = command, SDK = code.
AWS CAF = Business, People, Governance (business-focused) + Platform, Security, Operations (technical-focused).

💵 Module 2: Cloud Economics and Billing

Three cost drivers: compute, storage, data transfer.
Three pricing principles: pay for what you use, pay less when you reserve, pay less by using more.
TCO = direct + indirect costs; compares AWS against on-premises as a whole.
Pricing Calculator = before deployment (estimate); Cost Explorer = after/during (analyse); Budgets = alert against a target.
Support ladder: Basic → Developer → Business → Enterprise, scaled to business impact.

🌍 Module 3: AWS Global Infrastructure

Region = geographical area containing multiple Availability Zones.
Availability Zone = isolated infrastructure containing one or more data centres.
Edge location = nearby content-delivery point used by CloudFront.
Choose a Region using compliance, latency, service availability and cost.
VPC is Regional; a subnet belongs to one Availability Zone.
Data centre = physical facility inside an AZ; Points of Presence = edge locations + Regional edge caches.

🔐 Module 4: AWS Cloud Security

AWS = security OF the cloud; customer = security IN the cloud.
IAM user = long-term identity; group = users; policy = permissions; role = temporary assumable permissions.
Explicit Deny overrides Explicit Allow; otherwise access is implicitly denied.
Protect root, enable MFA, use individual identities and least privilege.
CloudTrail records actions; Config checks configuration; Artifact provides compliance reports.
Authentication proves identity; authorisation determines permissions.
At rest = stored data + KMS; in transit = moving data + TLS/HTTPS.

🌐 Module 5: Networking and Content Delivery

VPC spans a Region; each subnet belongs to one Availability Zone.
Public subnet = route to an internet gateway.
NAT gateway gives private resources outbound internet access.
Security group = stateful, instance level, allow only.
Network ACL = stateless, subnet level, allow and deny.

⚙️ Module 6: Compute

AMI = template; EC2 instance = running virtual machine.
IAM role grants AWS permissions; security group controls network traffic.
EBS persists; Instance Store is temporary.
On-Demand = uncertain, Reserved = predictable, Spot = interruptible, Dedicated Host = licensing.
ECS orchestrates AWS containers; EKS is Kubernetes; ECR stores images; Fargate runs containers without server management.

💾 Module 7: Storage

EBS = block storage for EC2; snapshots are point-in-time backups.
S3 = objects in buckets; designed for eleven nines of durability.
EFS = shared Linux file system using NFS and mount targets.
Glacier = archival storage with slower retrieval.
IOPS counts operations; throughput measures the amount of data transferred.

🗄️ Module 8: Databases

RDS = managed relational databases and transactions.
Multi-AZ = synchronous standby for availability; read replica = asynchronous copy for read scaling.
DynamoDB = NoSQL key-value/document data using partition and optional sort keys.
Redshift = analytical data warehouse using columnar storage and parallel processing.
Aurora = MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible relational engine managed through RDS.

EXAM PREPARATION

🧠 Dangerous Confusions

AWS distractors usually swap two services that solve nearby but different problems. Learn the boundary between them.

Pricing Calculator vs Cost Explorer

Pricing CalculatorBefore deployment — estimates a planned architecture.
Cost ExplorerAfter/during usage — analyses actual spending.

Cost Explorer vs Budgets

Cost Explorer"What happened to my costs?" — investigates.
AWS Budgets"Tell me when I approach a target." — alerts, doesn't block spending.

AWS Organizations vs IAM

OrganizationsCentral management of multiple AWS accounts.
IAMUsers, roles and permissions inside an account.

TAM vs Trusted Advisor vs Concierge

TAM / Trusted AdvisorProactive technical guidance / best-practice recommendations.
Support ConciergeAccount assistance — not technical guidance.

IaaS vs SaaS control

IaaSMost customer control — infrastructure provided, you manage more.
SaaSLeast customer control — finished software, provider manages almost everything.

Service model vs deployment model

Service modelIaaS/PaaS/SaaS — WHO manages WHAT.
Deployment modelCloud/Hybrid/On-premises — WHERE the environment lives.

Capital expense vs Variable expense

Capital expenseBuy infrastructure upfront, based on a forecast.
Variable expensePay according to actual usage as it occurs.

CAF Platform vs Operations

PlatformDesign and build the technical architecture.
OperationsRun, monitor and manage it day to day.

Region vs Availability Zone

RegionGeographic area containing multiple AZs.
Availability ZoneIsolated infrastructure within one Region.

Availability Zone vs data centre

Availability ZoneIsolated infrastructure partition within a Region.
Data centreThe physical facility inside an AZ; an AZ consists of one or more.

Multi-AZ vs Multi-Region

Multi-AZSeveral isolated locations inside one Region.
Multi-RegionSeparate geographical Regions entirely.

Elasticity vs Scalability

ElasticityAdjusts capacity up and down with current demand.
ScalabilityAbility to grow for a larger workload.

CloudTrail vs CloudWatch

CloudTrailWho performed which API action?
CloudWatchHow is the system performing?

Security group vs Network ACL

Security groupInstance level, stateful, allow only.
Network ACLSubnet level, stateless, allow and deny.

Internet gateway vs NAT gateway

Internet gatewayDirect public connectivity.
NAT gatewayOutbound internet for private resources.

IAM role vs Security group

IAM rolePermission to call AWS APIs.
Security groupPermission for network traffic.

AMI vs EC2 instance

AMITemplate or blueprint.
EC2 instanceRunning virtual machine created from the AMI.

ECS vs EKS vs ECR vs Fargate

ECS / EKSOrchestration: AWS-native / Kubernetes.
ECR / FargateImage storage / serverless container compute.

EBS vs EFS vs S3

EBS / EFSBlock disk / shared file system.
S3Object storage in buckets.

Multi-AZ vs Read Replica

Multi-AZHigh availability and failover.
Read replicaRead performance and scaling.

RDS vs Redshift

RDSRuns daily transactions.
RedshiftAnalyses historical data.

Route 53 vs CloudFront

Route 53Finds and routes to a destination.
CloudFrontCaches and delivers content near users.

IAM vs Amazon Cognito

IAMControls AWS workforce and workload identities, roles and permissions.
Amazon CognitoSupports application end-user sign-up, sign-in and identity flows.

Encryption at rest vs in transit

At restStored data is protected with encryption and keys, commonly managed through KMS.
In transitData moving across a network is protected with TLS or HTTPS.

AWS QUESTION LOGIC

🎯 How to Attack the Test

The test usually rewards precise service selection and punishes one swapped word. Read the requirement before reacting to a familiar service name.

Four-step question method

  1. Underline the actual requirement: availability, read scaling, archival, low latency or operating-system control.
  2. Identify the service category before choosing a service.
  3. Eliminate answers that solve a nearby but different problem.
  4. Choose the option that satisfies every stated requirement with the least unnecessary management.

Watch the command words

  • BEST / MOST: several answers may work, but only one is the intended fit.
  • Select TWO: select the complete set and nothing extra.
  • Managed / least operational effort: prefer the managed service over EC2.
  • Full control / custom OS: EC2 is often the clue.

Responsibility questions

  • Physical facilities, hardware and virtualisation → AWS.
  • Customer data, IAM, configuration and EC2 guest OS → customer.
  • The more managed the service, the more AWS operates underneath it.

Final-hour revision

  1. Read the master cheat sheet.
  2. Review dangerous confusions.
  3. Take one 30-question mixed test.
  4. Retry mistakes only.
  5. Open full notes only for concepts still unclear.

MODULE 1 · GUIDED LESSON 1 OF 5

☁️ Why Cloud Computing Exists

Before any service names, understand the problem cloud computing solves: companies were forced to guess how much hardware to buy, months before they actually needed it.

THE BIG STORY

QuickMart wants to launch an online store

In the traditional world, management says "we need servers." That single sentence sets off a long chain: estimate traffic, choose servers, get budget approval, order hardware, wait for delivery, install, configure, maintain. It can take weeks or months — and the original estimate may still be completely wrong.

1
Guess the demandForecast traffic months in advance, long before real usage exists.
2
Buy and waitApproval, procurement, delivery and installation can take weeks.
3
Cloud flips itRequest the resource now instead of forecasting and purchasing first.
4
Pay for usageSpend follows actual consumption instead of an upfront guess.

The three keywords

The module's core definition: cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute power, databases, storage, applications and other IT resources via the internet, with pay-as-you-go pricing. Three phrases explain almost all of it.

ON DEMAND VIA THE INTERNET PAY AS YOU GO

On demand

Request a resource and receive it now, without buying physical hardware first.

Traditional: "Submit purchase request. Wait." Cloud: "Create five virtual servers now." That speed becomes one of the six advantages later in the module.

Via the internet

Resources do not need to sit physically inside your company's building.

Your laptop reaches AWS over the internet, and AWS serves the server, database or storage back. You are consuming IT infrastructure as a service, remotely.

Pay-as-you-go

Pay according to usage instead of purchasing a large amount of hardware upfront.

Traditional: buy the server first, use it later. Cloud: use the resource, then pay for what was used. Module 2 expands this financial idea much further.

Infrastructure as hardware

A server is a physical thing. Getting another one means:

  • Buy it, ship it, rack it, wire it
  • Configure it, then maintain it
  • Space, staff and physical security

Infrastructure as software

A virtual server can instead be created through:

  • Console, command, script or API
  • Faster to deploy and easier to modify
  • Easier to automate, more flexible

Guess wrong, pay for it

The overprovisioning / underprovisioning problem this whole chapter exists to solve:

Buy too much: Demand: ████ Capacity: ████████████ Unused: ████████ → money wasted Buy too little: Demand: ████████████ Capacity: ████ → site struggles or fails

Exam lens

  • "Undifferentiated heavy lifting" means generic infrastructure work (replacing drives, cooling, wiring) that is necessary but does not make a retailer a better retailer.
  • Cloud does not mean free — it means pay-as-you-go, not pay-nothing.
  • Cloud does not mean infrastructure disappears — AWS still owns physical infrastructure; you consume it as a service instead of owning the hardware yourself.

Quick check

QuickMart's engineers spend a lot of time replacing broken hard drives and maintaining cooling systems. Is that effort part of what makes QuickMart a better retailer?

No. That is undifferentiated heavy lifting — necessary infrastructure work that does not itself differentiate the business. AWS's argument is to spend more effort on what makes the business unique and less on generic infrastructure.
MODULE 1 · GUIDED LESSON 2 OF 5

🧱 Renting a Kitchen: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS

Three cloud service models describe one question: how much do you manage yourself, and how much does the provider manage for you?

THE KITCHEN ANALOGY

IaaS rents you a kitchen. SaaS serves you dinner.

IaaS gives you the building, gas, electricity, oven and fridge — but you cook the food. PaaS is a restaurant kitchen where much more is already prepared, so you focus mainly on your recipe. SaaS means you don't cook at all: you go to the restaurant and eat the finished dish.

Control spectrum

Move down the list and the provider manages more; you manage less. Move up and it reverses.

MORE CONTROL IaaS ↓ PaaS ↓ SaaS LESS CONTROL MORE YOU MANAGE → IaaS LESS YOU MANAGE → SaaS

IaaS — Infrastructure as a Service

The provider supplies infrastructure; the customer manages most of the system.

AWS example: Amazon EC2. AWS provides the underlying infrastructure and virtual machine, but you retain substantial control over the operating system and configuration. Use when you need OS control or custom software installed.

PaaS — Platform as a Service

The provider manages more of the underlying environment; the customer focuses on the application and data.

AWS example: AWS Elastic Beanstalk. The idea: "I want to deploy my application without spending as much effort managing the underlying infrastructure."

SaaS — Software as a Service

A complete, finished application delivered to the user; the provider manages almost everything underneath.

You normally don't manage the server, operating system, runtime or application infrastructure — you simply use the software through a browser.

Exam lens

"More control usually also means more responsibility" — this becomes critical later in AWS security (shared responsibility). And don't confuse this with where something runs: service model asks how much you manage; deployment model (next lesson) asks where the environment lives.

SCENARIO A

"The company wants maximum control over the operating system and virtual server."

IaaS. Maximum infrastructure and OS control points to Infrastructure as a Service.
SCENARIO B

"Developers want to focus on application code instead of managing infrastructure."

PaaS. The provider manages more underneath so developers can focus on the app.
SCENARIO C

"Users simply access a finished application through the internet."

SaaS. A complete application consumed as-is, with least infrastructure control.

Quick check

True or false: "IaaS gives less control than SaaS."

False — it's backwards. Most control → IaaS. Least control → SaaS. This is one of the module's most common exam traps.
MODULE 1 · GUIDED LESSON 3 OF 5

🏢 Where It Runs, and Why It's Worth It

Deployment models answer WHERE the environment lives. The six advantages answer WHY a company bothers moving at all — probably the most examinable part of Module 1.

DON'T MIX THESE UP

Service model vs deployment model

IaaS/PaaS/SaaS asks who manages what. Cloud/Hybrid/On-premises asks where the computing environment exists. Students frequently confuse these two independent questions — they answer completely different exam clues.

Cloud deployment

Workloads deployed entirely in a cloud environment such as AWS.

The company does not need to host all the underlying physical infrastructure itself: Company → Internet → AWS Cloud.

Hybrid deployment

Some workloads stay on-premises and some use the cloud.

Example: a bank keeps sensitive legacy databases in its own data centre while running new web applications and analytics on AWS. Hybrid ≠ using two AWS services — it always means cloud + on-premises.

On-premises / private cloud

The organisation operates the infrastructure — servers, storage, network — within its own environment.

More direct control, but also far more infrastructure responsibility: hardware, physical security and maintenance all fall on the organisation.

Exam lens

AWS is not alien compared to traditional IT — it changes how things are delivered and managed, not what exists. Firewalls/routers/servers/storage/databases still exist conceptually as security groups, network ACLs, VPC, EC2, EBS, EFS, S3, RDS and IAM.

THE MOST EXAMINABLE PART OF MODULE 1

Six advantages of cloud computing

Know what each one actually means, not just the ritual chant. Memory shortcut: MONEY · SCALE · CAPACITY · SPEED · DATA CENTER · GLOBAL.

💰
1. Money — CapEx → variable expense

Trade large upfront capital expenditure for paying based on actual consumption.

📦
2. Scale — economies of scale

AWS aggregates enormous demand across customers, potentially passing savings on.

📊
3. Capacity — stop guessing

Scale resources up and down instead of forecasting a fixed maximum years ahead.

⚡
4. Speed — agility

Provision resources in minutes instead of waiting weeks for hardware.

🏭
5. Data center — stop maintaining it

Redirect staff and budget from generic infrastructure upkeep to the actual business.

🌎
6. Global — go global in minutes

Deploy resources in other AWS geographic locations far faster than building your own.

Traditional (CapEx)

QuickMart buys a server farm before earning anything:

RM500,000 servers RM100,000 networking RM100,000 storage RM50,000 installation

Cloud (variable expense)

Use resources, then pay based on consumption. If QuickMart fails after six months, it isn't left owning 100 idle servers — it simply stops using resources.

Use resources ↓ Pay based on consumption

Advantage 3 in one picture

Overestimate: capacity purchased > demand → idle infrastructure, wasted money Underestimate: capacity purchased < demand → poor performance, insufficient capacity Cloud: capacity follows demand → scale up when it rises, scale down when it falls
CLUE

"The company does not want to purchase expensive servers upfront."

Trade capital expense for variable expense.
CLUE

"Traffic changes significantly during the year."

Stop guessing capacity. Also the logic behind the module's own sample question: EC2 is economical for varying workloads because instances launch on demand.
CLUE

"The development team currently waits weeks for new servers."

Increase speed and agility.
CLUE

"IT staff should focus on customers instead of server maintenance."

Stop spending money running and maintaining data centers.
CLUE

"Why can a large provider offer lower unit costs than one company's own data centre?"

Massive economies of scale.
CLUE

"Expand the application from Malaysia to Europe and the US quickly."

Go global in minutes.

Exam lens

The six advantages are not all just "cheaper." Money covers CapEx→variable expense and economies of scale; the rest are about speed, capacity, operational focus and global reach. "Stop guessing capacity" also doesn't mean capacity planning disappears entirely — it means capacity can adjust dynamically instead of being locked to a long-term guess.

Quick check

A bank keeps its legacy databases in its own data centre but runs new customer-facing apps on AWS. What deployment model is this?

Hybrid — some workloads remain on-premises while others use the cloud. This is extremely common because organisations rarely migrate their entire IT estate at once.
MODULE 1 · GUIDED LESSON 4 OF 5

🧩 AWS as a Box of LEGO

AWS is a secure cloud platform offering a broad set of global services that are designed to work together like building blocks — not one enormous product.

THE LEGO ANALOGY

You choose the pieces, then combine them

EC2 for compute, S3 for storage, RDS for a database, VPC for networking, IAM for security — you combine the pieces to build an application. The service you pick depends on business goals and technology requirements, not on any one service being universally "best."

A simple AWS architecture

Page 26's example, grouped by category:

Users ↓ Amazon VPC → Networking ↓ Amazon EC2 → Compute ↓ Amazon DynamoDB → Database ↓ Amazon S3 → Storage

Choosing a service is like choosing a vehicle

"Which is better: EC2 or Lambda?" is like asking "which is better: a truck or a motorcycle?" For transporting 20 tonnes, the truck wins. For slipping through city traffic, probably not the truck. The requirement determines the service — there is no universally best AWS service.

A web service is software available over the internet using standard formats such as XML or JSON for API request-response interactions — this is why AWS can be controlled through APIs, not only through graphical screens.

Important AWS service map

NeedThink
Virtual serverEC2
Object storageS3
Block storageEBS
Shared file storageEFS
Relational databaseRDS
NoSQL databaseDynamoDB
Private networkVPC
PermissionsIAM
DNSRoute 53
Content deliveryCloudFront
MonitoringCloudWatch
Audit activityCloudTrail
Cost analysisCost Explorer

AWS Management Console

Think: Click. A graphical browser interface for configuring AWS resources.

Good for beginners, manual configuration and visual interaction.

AWS CLI

Think: Command. Command Line Interface — execute commands instead of clicking.

Useful for automation, scripts and repeatable administrative tasks.

AWS SDK

Think: Code. Software Development Kit — lets application code interact directly with AWS.

Available for languages such as Java and Python, so an application can programmatically store a file in S3, create a resource, or read a database record.

SCENARIO

"A developer wants to automate AWS operations through Python code."

SDK. Application code interacting directly with AWS.
SCENARIO

"An administrator wants to run AWS commands in shell scripts."

CLI. Commands and scripts, useful for automation.
SCENARIO

"A beginner wants to configure AWS using a graphical interface."

Management Console. Click-based, visual configuration.

Quick check

A colleague asks: "which is better, EC2 or Lambda?" What's wrong with the question?

It's incomplete. There is no universally best AWS service — the correct choice depends on the workload's business goals and technology requirements, just like choosing between a truck and a motorcycle depends on the cargo and the road.
MODULE 1 · GUIDED LESSON 5 OF 5

🗺️ AWS CAF: Moving More Than Just Servers

Cloud adoption is not merely "move the servers" — it affects finance, HR, security, management, operations and governance. AWS CAF organises that whole problem into six perspectives.

BUILDING A NEW DIGITAL CITY

Different departments ask different questions

AWS CAF provides guidance and best practices to help an organisation prepare for cloud adoption from both business and technical perspectives. The six perspectives split into two groups: Business, People and Governance are business-focused; Platform, Security and Operations are technical-focused.

The six questions

Memorise these six questions before the long capability lists — everything else is detail on top.

BUSINESS → Why are we moving? PEOPLE → Who needs skills and change? GOVERNANCE → What rules and oversight do we need? PLATFORM → What will we build? SECURITY → How will we protect it? OPERATIONS → How will we run it?

BUSINESS-FOCUSED

💼
Business

Does this investment help the business? IT finance, IT strategy, benefits realization, business risk.

🎓
People

Do employees have the skills? Staffing, training, career management, organisational change.

📋
Governance

How do we align projects with strategy and control risk? Portfolio, programme and licence management.

TECHNICAL-FOCUSED

🏗️
Platform

What do we build? Compute, network, storage and database provisioning; solution architecture.

🛡️
Security

How do we protect it? Identity and access management, data protection, incident response.

⚙️
Operations

How do we run it daily? Monitoring, change management, business continuity, disaster recovery.

SCENARIO

Finance wants to know whether cloud investment produces measurable business value.

Business.
SCENARIO

Staff need AWS training before migration begins.

People.
SCENARIO

Management wants cloud projects aligned with strategy and controlled through project governance.

Governance.
SCENARIO

Architects are designing compute, storage, networking and databases.

Platform.
SCENARIO

The company needs identity controls, data protection and incident-response procedures.

Security.
SCENARIO

The organisation needs monitoring, change management and disaster recovery.

Operations.

Exam lens

  • AWS CAF is not just a technical architecture diagram — half its perspectives in this module are business-focused.
  • Platform ≠ Operations. Platform designs/builds the architecture; Operations runs/monitors/manages it day to day.
  • Business ≠ Governance. Business is about value, finance and strategy; Governance is about oversight, alignment, projects and measurement.

Quick check

An organisation has finished building its AWS architecture. Now it needs to monitor applications and recover quickly if something fails. Which CAF perspective covers this?

Operations. "How will this environment be run every day after we build it?" covers monitoring, change management, reporting and disaster recovery — distinct from Platform, which covers designing and building the architecture in the first place.

Module 1 is basically the “why cloud exists” chapter.

Before AWS teaches you EC2, S3, VPC, IAM, databases, and all the alphabet soup, this module answers four bigger questions:

  1. What is cloud computing?
  2. Why would a company use cloud instead of its own data center?
  3. What exactly is AWS?
  4. How does a company actually prepare itself to move to the cloud?

Those are exactly the four major sections in the module.

1. Start with the big idea

Imagine a company called QuickMart.

QuickMart wants to launch an online store.

In the traditional world, management might say:

“We need servers.”

So the IT team must:

Estimate how much traffic will come
↓
Choose servers
↓
Get budget approval
↓
Order hardware
↓
Wait for delivery
↓
Install servers
↓
Configure networking
↓
Install operating systems
↓
Maintain everything

That may take weeks or months.

And the really amusing part is that their original estimate may be completely wrong.

If they buy too much:

Demand:
████

Capacity:
████████████

Unused:
████████

Money is wasted.

If they buy too little:

Demand:
████████████

Capacity:
████

Result:
Site struggles or fails

Cloud computing exists largely because companies got tired of playing this very expensive guessing game.

2. What is cloud computing?

The module gives a very important definition:

Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute power, databases, storage, applications, and other IT resources via the internet, with pay-as-you-go pricing.

There are three phrases you should absolutely notice:

ON DEMAND
VIA THE INTERNET
PAY AS YOU GO

Those three phrases explain most of cloud computing.

3. What does “on demand” mean?

Suppose QuickMart suddenly needs five servers.

Traditional approach:

“Submit purchase request. Wait. Procurement is investigating the emotional state of the invoice.”

Cloud:

“Create five virtual servers now.”

That is on-demand access.

You don't normally need to buy a physical server first.

Conceptually:

Need resource
↓
Request resource
↓
Resource becomes available

That speed becomes one of the major cloud advantages later in the chapter.

4. What does “via the internet” mean?

The resources do not need to physically sit inside your company's building.

You can access computing services remotely.

For example:

Your laptop
    ↓
Internet
    ↓
AWS
    ↓
Server / database / storage

You are consuming IT infrastructure as a service.

5. What does “pay-as-you-go” mean?

Instead of necessarily purchasing a large amount of hardware before you know how much you need, cloud lets you pay based more closely on usage.

Traditional:

Buy server first
↓
Use it later

Cloud:

Use resource
↓
Pay for usage

This is the financial idea that Module 2 expands much further.

6. Infrastructure as hardware vs infrastructure as software

Page 7 introduces one of the best conceptual ideas in the module:

Cloud computing lets you stop thinking of infrastructure only as hardware and instead think of it as software.

This sounds abstract, but it is actually simple.

Traditional infrastructure

Suppose you need another server.

A server is a physical thing.

You might need to:

Buy it
Ship it
Rack it
Wire it
Configure it
Maintain it

Cloud infrastructure

A virtual server can instead be created through:

Console
Command
Script
API

So infrastructure begins behaving more like software.

7. Why “infrastructure as software” matters

Imagine increasing capacity.

Hardware world

You want 20 additional servers.

That involves physical procurement.

Cloud world

You can create additional resources programmatically.

This means infrastructure can become:

  • faster to deploy;
  • easier to modify;
  • easier to automate;
  • more flexible.

The module contrasts the traditional computing model with cloud specifically in this way. Traditional infrastructure requires space, staff, physical security, planning and capital expenditure, while cloud infrastructure can change more quickly and flexibly.

8. “Undifferentiated heavy lifting”

Page 9 says cloud can eliminate undifferentiated heavy-lifting tasks.

That phrase sounds like AWS hired a philosopher, but the idea is straightforward.

QuickMart wants to sell products.

Its competitive advantage probably does not come from:

Replacing broken hard drives
Installing rack equipment
Maintaining cooling systems
Running electrical infrastructure

Those things are necessary.

But they do not make QuickMart a better retailer.

AWS's argument is:

Spend more effort on what makes your business unique, and less effort maintaining generic infrastructure.

Section 1B: Cloud service models

9. IaaS, PaaS and SaaS

The module introduces three cloud service models:

IaaS
PaaS
SaaS

The central difference is:

How much do you manage yourself?

Page 10 shows the spectrum from more control to less control.

The easiest analogy is food.

10. IaaS — Infrastructure as a Service

Imagine renting a kitchen.

The kitchen gives you:

Building
Gas
Electricity
Oven
Fridge

But you cook the food.

That is roughly IaaS.

The cloud provider gives you infrastructure.

You still manage many things yourself.

Example later in AWS:

Amazon EC2

With EC2, AWS provides the underlying infrastructure and virtual machine, but you still have substantial control over the operating system and configuration.

Memory:

IaaS
= infrastructure provided
= most control of the three

11. PaaS — Platform as a Service

Now imagine a restaurant kitchen where much more is already prepared.

You mainly focus on:

Your recipe
Your application
Your data

rather than building and maintaining the kitchen.

That is PaaS.

AWS examples you encounter later include services such as:

AWS Elastic Beanstalk

The idea is:

“I want to deploy my application without spending as much effort managing the underlying infrastructure.”

Memory:

PaaS
= focus more on the application
= provider manages more underneath

12. SaaS — Software as a Service

Now imagine you do not cook at all.

You just go to the restaurant and eat.

The entire application is delivered to you.

That is SaaS.

Examples outside AWS might include services you simply use through a browser.

You normally do not manage:

Server
Operating system
Runtime
Application infrastructure

You simply use the software.

Memory:

SaaS
= finished software
= least infrastructure control

13. Service model spectrum

The clean mental picture is:

MORE CONTROL
     ↓

IaaS
↓
PaaS
↓
SaaS

     ↓
LESS CONTROL

But the other side of that is:

MORE YOU MANAGE
IaaS

LESS YOU MANAGE
SaaS

This becomes extremely important later in AWS security because more control usually also means more responsibility.

14. IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS scenario thinking

If a question says:

“The company wants maximum control over the operating system and virtual server.”

Think:

IaaS

If it says:

“Developers want to focus on application code instead of managing the underlying infrastructure.”

Think:

PaaS

If it says:

“Users simply access a finished application.”

Think:

SaaS

Section 1C: Deployment models

15. Cloud deployment models

The module teaches three deployment models:

Cloud
Hybrid
On-premises / private cloud

These answer a different question from IaaS/PaaS/SaaS.

Service models ask:

What level of service are you consuming?

Deployment models ask:

Where does the computing environment live?

Students often mix those up.

16. Cloud deployment

In a cloud model, workloads are deployed in a cloud environment such as AWS.

Conceptually:

Company
   ↓
Internet
   ↓
AWS Cloud

The company does not need to host all the underlying physical infrastructure itself.

17. On-premises / private cloud

This means the organisation operates the infrastructure within its own environment.

Conceptually:

Company building
│
├── Servers
├── Storage
├── Network
└── Private infrastructure

The organisation keeps more direct control but also carries much more infrastructure responsibility.

18. Hybrid deployment

Hybrid means:

Some workloads stay on-premises and some use the cloud.

Example:

Company data center
        ↕
      Network
        ↕
     AWS Cloud

This is extremely common conceptually because organisations rarely wake up on Tuesday and teleport their entire IT estate into AWS by lunch.

19. When would hybrid make sense?

Imagine a bank.

It may have:

Old internal systems
Sensitive legacy databases
Existing data center infrastructure

But it also wants:

Cloud scalability
New applications
Cloud backups
Analytics

So it uses both.

That is hybrid.

20. Don't confuse service model and deployment model

This distinction is exam-worthy.

IaaS / PaaS / SaaS
→ WHO manages WHAT

Cloud / Hybrid / On-premises
→ WHERE the environment exists

21. AWS is not completely alien compared with traditional IT

Page 12 gives a very useful comparison between traditional IT and AWS.

Traditional IT has:

Firewalls
Routers
Servers
Storage
Databases
Administrators

AWS has equivalent cloud concepts such as:

Security groups
Network ACLs
Amazon VPC
Amazon EC2
Amazon EBS
Amazon EFS
Amazon S3
Amazon RDS
IAM

So cloud computing does not erase the ideas of networking, servers, storage and security.

It changes how those things are delivered and managed.

Section 2: Six advantages of cloud computing

This is probably one of the most examinable parts of Module 1.

The six advantages are:

  1. Trade capital expense for variable expense
  2. Benefit from massive economies of scale
  3. Stop guessing capacity
  4. Increase speed and agility
  5. Stop spending money running and maintaining data centers
  6. Go global in minutes

You should know what each one actually means, not just chant them like an AWS ritual.

22. Advantage 1 — Trade capital expense for variable expense

Traditional IT often requires capital expenditure.

Suppose QuickMart wants a server farm.

Before earning anything, it might spend:

RM500,000 servers
RM100,000 networking
RM100,000 storage
RM50,000 installation

That is a major upfront investment.

Cloud shifts toward variable expense.

Instead of buying everything upfront:

Use resources
↓
Pay based on consumption

The page 15 diagram contrasts investment based on forecasts with paying for what is consumed.

Memory:

CAPEX
= buy infrastructure upfront

VARIABLE EXPENSE
= pay as usage occurs

23. Why this is useful

Imagine QuickMart fails after six months.

On-premises

It may still own:

100 servers
Network equipment
Storage equipment

which it no longer needs.

Cloud

It can stop resources and reduce future usage.

So cloud decreases the need to gamble large amounts of money on uncertain future demand.

24. Advantage 2 — Massive economies of scale

AWS serves huge numbers of customers.

Because of that aggregate demand, AWS operates at a much larger scale than one ordinary company could.

Page 16 says AWS can achieve economies of scale and pass savings to customers.

Think wholesale purchasing.

A person buying:

1 server

has little purchasing leverage.

AWS operates enormous infrastructure.

So its per-unit economics can be different.

Memory:

Huge AWS scale
↓
Lower unit economics
↓
Potential savings for customers

25. Advantage 3 — Stop guessing capacity

This one is particularly important.

With traditional infrastructure, companies must forecast future demand.

Suppose QuickMart predicts:

Expected peak:
10,000 users

If it prepares capacity for:

20,000 users

it overestimates.

Money is wasted.

If it prepares for:

5,000 users

it underestimates.

Performance suffers.

The slide on page 17 explicitly contrasts overestimated capacity, underestimated capacity, and scaling on demand.

26. Cloud solution to capacity guessing

Cloud allows capacity to scale more dynamically.

Conceptually:

Low demand
→ fewer resources

High demand
→ more resources

Demand falls
→ reduce resources

So instead of guessing the theoretical maximum years in advance, the system can adapt more closely to real demand.

27. Advantage 4 — Increase speed and agility

Traditional infrastructure:

Need server
↓
Approval
↓
Purchase
↓
Delivery
↓
Installation
↓
Configuration

Weeks

Cloud:

Need server
↓
Launch

Minutes

Page 18 literally contrasts weeks with minutes.

That speed matters because developers can experiment faster.

28. Why agility matters to business

Suppose QuickMart wants to test a new recommendation engine.

Traditional environment:

“Infrastructure will be ready in six weeks.”

The idea may already be irrelevant by then.

Cloud:

“Create the resources today.”

That makes experimentation cheaper and faster.

So agility is not just an IT benefit.

It can become a business advantage.

29. Advantage 5 — Stop spending money running data centers

A data center costs more than servers.

Page 19 illustrates costs such as:

Payroll
Utilities
Maintenance
Landscaping
Hardware

The idea is that organisations can redirect resources away from generic infrastructure operation and toward their actual business.

For QuickMart:

Less effort:
"How do we cool this server room?"

More effort:
"How do we improve customer experience?"

That is the real business argument.

30. Advantage 6 — Go global in minutes

Suppose QuickMart starts in Malaysia.

Then it gets customers in:

Europe
United States
Japan
Australia

Traditional approach might require setting up international infrastructure.

Cloud lets the company deploy workloads in other AWS geographical locations far more quickly.

The page 20 diagram shows a world map and deployment across AWS Regions.

Memory:

New geographic market
↓
Deploy resources closer to users
↓
Global reach faster

31. The six advantages as one story

Imagine QuickMart moves to AWS.

Before cloud

Buy hardware upfront
Guess future demand
Wait weeks for servers
Maintain data center
Expand internationally slowly

Management discovers this is expensive and inflexible.

With cloud

Pay based on consumption
Use AWS economies of scale
Scale according to demand
Launch resources quickly
Avoid much data-center heavy lifting
Deploy globally faster

That single before/after story covers all six advantages.

32. Six advantages memory shortcut

You can remember them as:

MONEY
SCALE
CAPACITY
SPEED
DATA CENTER
GLOBAL

Expanded:

Money
→ CapEx to variable expense

Scale
→ Economies of scale

Capacity
→ Stop guessing

Speed
→ Agility

Data center
→ Stop maintaining everything yourself

Global
→ Deploy worldwide quickly

Section 3: What is AWS?

33. AWS in simple terms

The module defines AWS as a secure cloud platform offering a broad set of global cloud-based products.

It provides on-demand access to things such as:

Compute
Storage
Networking
Database
Management tools

and AWS services are designed to work together like building blocks.

That building-block analogy is excellent.

34. AWS as LEGO

Imagine AWS as a giant box of LEGO.

You may choose:

EC2 → Compute
S3 → Storage
RDS → Database
VPC → Networking
IAM → Security / access

You combine the pieces to build an application.

AWS is not one enormous product.

It is a collection of services.

35. Simple AWS architecture

Page 26 shows a simple architecture consisting of:

Users
↓
Amazon VPC
↓
Amazon EC2
↓
Amazon DynamoDB
↓
Amazon S3

The diagram groups them by categories:

Networking → VPC
Compute    → EC2
Database   → DynamoDB
Storage    → S3

This is worth understanding because later modules simply zoom in on each block.

36. Core categories you should recognise

The slides list many categories, but for Cloud Foundations, some especially important ones are:

Compute
Storage
Database
Networking and Content Delivery
Security, Identity and Compliance
Management and Governance
Cost Management

The module then lists the specific services covered later in the course.

37. Important AWS service map

A useful mental map:

NeedThink
Virtual serverEC2
Object storageS3
Block storageEBS
Shared file storageEFS
Relational databaseRDS
NoSQL databaseDynamoDB
Private networkVPC
PermissionsIAM
DNSRoute 53

MonitoringCloudWatch

Cost analysisCost Explorer

You will learn the details in later modules.

Module 1 only wants you to understand that AWS has categories and services that work together.

38. Choosing an AWS service

Page 27 gives a crucial rule:

The service selected depends on business goals and technology requirements.

There is no universally “best AWS service.”

Example:

“Which is better: EC2 or Lambda?”

That question is incomplete.

It depends on the workload.

It is like asking:

“Which is better: a truck or a motorcycle?”

For transporting 20 tonnes?

Truck.

For slipping through Kuala Lumpur traffic?

Probably not the truck.

The requirement determines the service.

39. What is a web service?

Page 23 defines a web service as software available over the internet that uses standard formats such as XML or JSON for API request-response interactions.

Think:

Client
   ↓ request
Internet
   ↓
Web service
   ↓ response
Client

This is important because AWS services can be controlled through APIs rather than only through graphical screens.

40. Three ways to interact with AWS

The module teaches three primary ways:

AWS Management Console
AWS CLI
AWS SDKs

41. AWS Management Console

This is the graphical interface.

Think:

Browser
↓
Click buttons
↓
Configure AWS resources

Good for:

Beginners
Manual configuration
Visual interaction

Memory:

Console
= GUI

42. AWS CLI

CLI means Command Line Interface.

Instead of clicking:

Create instance

you execute commands.

This is useful for:

Automation
Scripts
Repeatable tasks

Memory:

CLI
= commands/scripts

43. AWS SDK

SDK means Software Development Kit.

This lets application code interact directly with AWS.

Examples from the module include languages such as:

Java
Python

So your application can programmatically say:

Store this file in S3
Create a resource
Read a database record

Memory:

SDK
= AWS from your application code

44. Console vs CLI vs SDK

Easy comparison:

MethodThink
Management ConsoleClick
CLIType command
SDKWrite code

If a question says:

“A developer wants to automate AWS operations through Python code.”

Think:

SDK

If it says:

“An administrator wants to execute AWS commands in scripts.”

Think:

CLI

If it says:

“A user wants a graphical interface.”

Think:

Management Console

Section 4: AWS Cloud Adoption Framework

This is the part students often memorize badly.

AWS CAF is easier if you understand the problem it is trying to solve.

45. Why does AWS CAF exist?

Suppose QuickMart says:

“We are moving to AWS tomorrow.”

The IT team may be ready.

But what about:

Finance?
HR?
Security?
Management?
Operations?
Governance?
Training?
Policies?
Business strategy?

Cloud adoption is not merely:

“Move the servers.”

It affects the entire organisation.

The module says AWS CAF provides guidance and best practices to help organisations build a comprehensive approach to cloud adoption.

46. AWS CAF in one sentence

AWS CAF helps an organisation prepare for cloud adoption from both business and technical perspectives.

The module organises AWS CAF into six perspectives.

47. The six AWS CAF perspectives

The version taught in this 2022 module uses:

Business
People
Governance
Platform
Security
Operations

The slide groups them into two broad sides.

Business-focused

Business
People
Governance

Technical-focused

Platform
Security
Operations

That grouping is extremely useful.

48. AWS CAF as building a new city

Imagine QuickMart is not just moving servers.

It is building a new digital city.

Different groups ask different questions.

49. Business perspective

The Business perspective asks:

“Does this cloud investment actually help the business?”

It includes things such as:

IT finance
IT strategy
Benefits realization
Business risk management

Stakeholders in the slide include business managers, finance managers, budget owners and strategy stakeholders.

Think:

Money
Business value
Strategy
Return
Risk

Example:

“How will migrating to AWS improve profitability?”

That is mainly Business perspective.

50. People perspective

The People perspective asks:

“Do our employees have the skills and organisational structure needed for cloud?”

It includes:

Resource management
Incentive management
Career management
Training management
Organizational change management

Think:

Employees
Training
Staffing
Skills
Culture
Change

Example:

“Developers do not yet understand cloud technologies. We need training.”

People perspective

51. Governance perspective

The Governance perspective asks:

“How do we keep cloud adoption aligned with business strategy, projects, policies and risk?”

It includes:

Portfolio management
Program/project management
Business performance measurement
License management

Think:

Rules
Oversight
Projects
Measurement
Control
Risk

Example:

“Who ensures cloud projects remain aligned with corporate goals?”

Governance perspective

52. Platform perspective

The Platform perspective focuses on the technical architecture.

It includes:

Compute provisioning
Network provisioning
Storage provisioning
Database provisioning
Systems and solution architecture
Application development

Think:

What do we actually build?

Example:

“What networking, compute, database and storage architecture should we design?”

Platform perspective

53. Security perspective

The Security perspective asks:

“How do we meet security objectives?”

Capabilities include:

Identity and access management
Detective controls
Infrastructure security
Data protection
Incident response

Think:

Protect
Detect
Respond
Control access
Protect data

Example:

“How should employee access to AWS resources be controlled?”

Security perspective

54. Operations perspective

The Operations perspective asks:

“How will this environment be run every day after we build it?”

It includes:

Service monitoring
Application performance monitoring
Resource inventory management
Release/change management
Reporting and analytics
Business continuity/disaster recovery
IT service catalog

Think:

Day-to-day running
Monitoring
Maintenance
Recovery
Changes

Example:

“How do we monitor applications and recover from failures?”

Operations perspective

55. AWS CAF perspectives as six questions

This is probably the easiest way to memorize them:

BUSINESS
→ Why are we moving?

PEOPLE
→ Who needs skills and change?

GOVERNANCE
→ What rules and oversight do we need?

PLATFORM
→ What will we build?

SECURITY
→ How will we protect it?

OPERATIONS
→ How will we run it?

If you remember those six questions, CAF becomes far easier than memorising dozens of bullet points.

57. Common exam traps

Trap 1 — Cloud means “everything is free”

No.

The module explicitly emphasizes pay-as-you-go, not “pay nothing.”

Trap 2 — Cloud means no infrastructure exists

Also no.

AWS still owns physical infrastructure.

The difference is that you consume it as a service rather than necessarily owning the hardware yourself.

Trap 3 — Cloud automatically means SaaS

No.

Cloud services can be:

IaaS
PaaS
SaaS

Trap 4 — Hybrid means using two AWS services

No.

Hybrid refers to using both:

Cloud
+
On-premises environment

Trap 5 — IaaS gives less control than SaaS

Backwards.

Most control → IaaS
Least control → SaaS

Trap 6 — The six cloud advantages are all just “cheaper”

No.

Some are financial.

Others are about:

Speed
Agility
Capacity
Global reach
Operational focus

Trap 7 — “Stop guessing capacity” means capacity never needs planning

Not quite.

It means cloud allows capacity to adjust dynamically rather than requiring companies to lock in huge fixed physical capacity based solely on long-term guesses.

Trap 8 — Go global means one server automatically serves the world with perfect latency

No.

The idea is that AWS provides infrastructure in multiple geographic locations, making global deployment much faster.

Trap 9 — AWS CAF is a technical architecture diagram

No.

CAF is a framework for organisational cloud adoption.

It includes business, people and governance—not just technology.

Trap 10 — Platform and Operations are the same

No.

Platform
→ design/build architecture

Operations
→ run/monitor/manage it

Trap 11 — Business and Governance are the same

Not quite.

Business
→ business value, finance, strategy

Governance
→ oversight, alignment, projects, measurement

58. The sample question in the module

The module asks:

Why is AWS more economical than traditional data centers for applications with varying compute workloads?

The correct answer is:

Amazon EC2 instances can be launched on demand when needed.

Why?

Because the important keyword is:

varying workloads

If workload changes, AWS allows capacity to follow demand more closely.

The wrong answer saying:

“Run enough instances permanently for peak workload”

would recreate the exact traditional overprovisioning problem cloud is supposed to solve.

59. Subjective answer — What is cloud computing?

A good answer:

Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of IT resources such as compute power, storage, databases and applications over the internet using pay-as-you-go pricing. Instead of purchasing and maintaining all physical infrastructure upfront, organisations can request cloud resources when required and adjust them according to changing demand.

60. Subjective answer — Traditional vs cloud computing

In traditional computing, infrastructure is treated mainly as physical hardware that must be purchased, installed, maintained and planned in advance. This can involve long procurement cycles, large upfront capital expenditure and capacity forecasting. In cloud computing, infrastructure can be treated more like software because resources can be created, changed and removed programmatically. This gives organisations greater flexibility, faster provisioning and the ability to scale resources according to actual demand.

61. Subjective answer — Six advantages

The six main advantages of cloud computing are trading capital expense for variable expense, benefiting from economies of scale, stopping the need to guess capacity, increasing speed and agility, reducing the burden of running and maintaining data centers, and gaining the ability to deploy globally more quickly. Together, these advantages allow organisations to align infrastructure more closely with actual demand while focusing more resources on business value.

62. Subjective answer — AWS CAF

The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework provides guidance and best practices to help organisations plan and manage successful cloud adoption. The framework recognises that cloud migration affects not only technology but the entire organisation. In the module, AWS CAF is divided into six perspectives: Business, People, Governance, Platform, Security and Operations. Business, People and Governance focus mainly on business capabilities, while Platform, Security and Operations focus mainly on technical capabilities.

The single most important idea in Module 1

Module 1 is really teaching one shift:

OLD THINKING

"How much hardware should we buy now
for what we think we might need later?"

becomes:

CLOUD THINKING

"What resources do we need now,
and how can we adjust them as requirements change?"

Everything else in the chapter—pay-as-you-go pricing, elasticity, agility, global reach, service models, and even AWS CAF—grows out of that change in thinking.

MODULE 1 · SUBJECTIVE EXAM PREPARATION

✍️ Writing Answers That Earn Marks

Module 1's exam is subjective, not objective — there is no question bank here. You need to define the concept, explain why it matters, and apply it to the scenario in front of you.

The 4-move answer formula

1. Identify

Name the concept the scenario is actually testing.

2. Define

State what it means in one or two precise sentences.

3. Apply

Connect it directly to the details given in the scenario.

4. Conclude

Close with why that connection matters for the organisation.

Weak answer

"Cloud computing has elasticity."

Defines a term and stops. Never touches the scenario. This earns partial marks at best.

Strong answer

"One relevant advantage is that the organisation can stop guessing capacity. In a traditional environment, the retailer might purchase enough servers for peak holiday traffic even though those servers would remain underused the rest of the year. With cloud computing, resources can be increased when holiday demand rises and reduced afterward, which helps reduce overprovisioning and unnecessary cost."

That last sentence connecting back to the scenario is what separates a good answer from a definition dump.

Model-answer bank

LIKELY QUESTION

What is cloud computing?

Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of IT resources such as compute power, storage, databases and applications over the internet using pay-as-you-go pricing. Instead of purchasing and maintaining all physical infrastructure upfront, organisations can request cloud resources when required and adjust them according to changing demand.
LIKELY QUESTION

Traditional vs cloud computing

In traditional computing, infrastructure is treated mainly as physical hardware that must be purchased, installed, maintained and planned in advance — long procurement cycles, large capital expenditure, capacity forecasting. In cloud computing, infrastructure can be treated more like software because resources can be created, changed and removed programmatically, giving greater flexibility, faster provisioning and demand-based scaling.
LIKELY QUESTION

Differentiate IaaS, PaaS and SaaS

IaaS provides fundamental infrastructure such as virtual machines and gives customers the greatest control over the OS and configuration. PaaS provides a managed application platform so developers can focus more on application code while the provider manages more infrastructure. SaaS provides a complete software application consumed without managing the underlying platform. Customer control generally decreases from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS.
LIKELY QUESTION

Explain hybrid cloud

A hybrid deployment combines cloud infrastructure with an organisation's on-premises environment. Some applications or data remain on-premises while other workloads use cloud services — useful when an organisation must retain sensitive or legacy systems locally while still benefiting from cloud scalability and flexibility.
LIKELY QUESTION

Explain the benefits of cloud computing

Cloud computing provides several advantages over traditional computing. Organisations can trade large capital expenditure for variable expense by paying according to usage; cloud providers can achieve economies of scale; organisations do not need to predict maximum capacity far in advance because resources scale on demand; resources can be provisioned quickly, improving speed and agility; organisations can reduce the burden of operating physical data centres; and cloud infrastructure enables faster global deployment.
LIKELY QUESTION

Console vs CLI vs SDK

The Management Console provides a graphical interface accessed through a browser — think "click." The AWS CLI enables interaction through commands and scripts, useful for automation and repeatable tasks — think "command." AWS SDKs let application code interact directly with AWS from languages such as Python or Java — think "code," used when an application must call AWS programmatically.
LIKELY QUESTION

Explain AWS CAF

The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework provides guidance and best practices that help organisations prepare for successful cloud adoption, recognising that adoption affects the whole organisation, not only IT. It consists of six perspectives: Business, People, Governance, Platform, Security and Operations. Business, People and Governance focus mainly on business capabilities; Platform, Security and Operations focus mainly on technical capabilities.
CAF PERSPECTIVE

Business perspective — good answer

The Business perspective ensures IT strategy and cloud investments align with business needs and produce measurable business outcomes — IT finance, strategy, benefits realization and business risk.
CAF PERSPECTIVE

People perspective — good answer

The People perspective focuses on organisational skills, staffing, training and change management, preparing employees and organisational structures for successful cloud adoption.
CAF PERSPECTIVE

Governance perspective — good answer

The Governance perspective ensures cloud initiatives, IT strategy and business goals remain aligned — programme management, portfolio management, performance measurement and licence management to maximise value and reduce risk.
CAF PERSPECTIVE

Platform perspective — good answer

The Platform perspective focuses on designing and implementing the target cloud architecture — compute, network, storage and database provisioning, systems architecture and application development.
CAF PERSPECTIVE

Security perspective — good answer

The Security perspective ensures the organisation meets its security objectives — identity and access management, infrastructure security, data protection, detection and incident response.
CAF PERSPECTIVE

Operations perspective — good answer

The Operations perspective focuses on the ongoing operation and support of cloud workloads — monitoring, change management, resource management, reporting, business continuity and disaster recovery.

Scenario → concept drill

DRILL

A retailer has very high traffic only during holiday sales.

Stop guessing capacity. Scale up for the sale, scale down afterward — avoids permanent overprovisioning.
DRILL

A startup can't predict its future traffic and doesn't want to buy servers upfront.

Trade capital expense for variable expense (plus stop guessing capacity).
DRILL

A company wants full control over its virtual server's operating system.

IaaS. Maximum customer control over infrastructure.
DRILL

A bank keeps legacy systems on-premises but runs new apps on AWS.

Hybrid deployment.
DRILL

Finance asks whether the AWS migration produces measurable business value.

CAF Business perspective.
DRILL

The organisation needs monitoring, change management and disaster recovery processes.

CAF Operations perspective.

🧠
Common mistakes and dangerous confusionsThe 11 traps the module itself calls out, condensed.
⌄
  • Cloud ≠ free. It is pay-as-you-go, not pay-nothing.
  • Cloud ≠ no infrastructure exists. AWS still owns physical infrastructure; you consume it as a service.
  • Cloud ≠ automatically SaaS. Cloud services can be IaaS, PaaS or SaaS.
  • Hybrid ≠ using two AWS services. It means cloud + on-premises.
  • IaaS does not give less control than SaaS — it's the reverse. Most control → IaaS. Least control → SaaS.
  • The six advantages are not all just "cheaper." Some are about speed, agility, capacity and global reach, not only money.
  • "Stop guessing capacity" ≠ no capacity planning at all. It means capacity can adjust dynamically rather than being locked to a long-term guess.
  • "Go global in minutes" ≠ one server magically serves the world. AWS provides infrastructure in multiple locations, making global deployment much faster.
  • AWS CAF ≠ a technical architecture diagram. Business, People and Governance are just as central as Platform, Security and Operations.
  • Platform ≠ Operations. Platform designs/builds; Operations runs/monitors/manages.
  • Business ≠ Governance. Business is value, finance and strategy; Governance is oversight, alignment and measurement.
MODULE 2 · GUIDED LESSON 1 OF 5

💵 How AWS Actually Charges You

CloudMart owns a small data centre and wants to know: would moving to AWS be cheaper? That question takes the whole module to answer properly — it starts here, with what AWS actually bills for.

THE MODULE'S OWN FLOW

One question leads to the next

How AWS charges → is AWS cheaper than on-premises? → estimate before building → manage multiple accounts → monitor actual spending → get AWS support when needed. That chain is Module 2's five sections in order. This lesson covers the first link: the three cost drivers and AWS's three pricing principles.

1
How AWS chargesThree cost drivers: compute, storage, data transfer.
2
Is it cheaper?Total Cost of Ownership compares the whole picture, not just sticker price.
3
Estimate firstPricing Calculator predicts cost before anything is built.
4
Monitor afterBilling tools and support keep spending under control once it's live.

The restaurant analogy

AWS is more complicated than a restaurant, but the financial logic is surprisingly similar.

People cooking → Compute Space holding food → Storage Moving food around → Data transfer

Compute cost

Roughly: amount of compute × time used.

Charged according to how long it runs and the type of instance used. A small server at $0.02/hour running 10 hours costs $0.20 — the point isn't that it's free, it's that you pay for actual usage instead of buying a physical server first.

Storage cost

Typically charged per GB stored.

10 GB costs less than 10 TB, but cost also depends on the storage type chosen — S3 Standard, S3 Standard-IA, Glacier, EBS, EFS. Different tiers exist because paying premium prices for data you barely touch wastes money.

Data-transfer cost

Data IN → generally no charge, with exceptions. Data OUT → generally charged.

Think of AWS as a hotel: bringing luggage in is often free; shipping ten tonnes out across the world is where the bill shows up. "Large amounts of data transferred OUT" should immediately flag potential data-transfer cost.

🎯
Pay for what you use

Consume resources according to actual requirements instead of buying for peak demand upfront.

📅
Pay less when you reserve

Commit to predictable long-term usage (Reserved Instances) in exchange for a discount.

📦
Pay less by using more

Volume-based tiered pricing — S3, EBS, EFS — plus AWS's own economies of scale.

Traditional: buy for peak

Normal demand: ███ Peak demand: ██████████ Purchased: ██████████ Most of the year: ███ used, ███████ unused

The empty capacity does not politely refund itself.

AWS: follow demand

Normal: ███ Sale: ██████████ After: ███

Elasticity is also an economic idea, not merely a technical one.

Reserved Instance payment options

RI payment optionModule's idea
No UpfrontSmaller discount
Partial UpfrontLarger discount
All UpfrontLargest discount

Slide claims savings of up to 75% — treat as the module's historical statement, not a permanent guarantee.

Exam lens

  • A 40% discount on something you don't need is not a saving — reserving a large instance you didn't need still wastes money versus the small instance you actually needed.
  • "Use more → price per unit may fall" does not mean your total bill falls. Storing 1 PB instead of 10 GB does not become cheaper overall.
  • Free service ≠ free architecture. Elastic Beanstalk itself may carry no separate charge, but the EC2 instances, load balancer and storage it provisions still cost money.

Quick check

CloudMart knows an application will run continuously for the next three years. Should it use On-Demand pricing or consider a reservation?

Consider a reservation. Predictable, long-term workloads are exactly the pattern that earns a Reserved Instance discount — unpredictable workloads should stay on flexible pay-as-you-go pricing instead.
MODULE 2 · GUIDED LESSON 2 OF 5

🧮 Total Cost of Ownership

Comparing "price of AWS EC2" against "price of one physical server" is missing half the story. TCO is the financial estimate that captures the rest.

THE CAR ANALOGY

RM80,000 is not the total cost of owning a car

Fuel, insurance, road tax, tyres, maintenance, repairs, parking, depreciation — all on top. A RM20,000 server works the same way: TCO is not the price on the box. The important word is TOTAL, covering both direct and indirect costs of owning and operating a system.

🖥️
Server costs

Hardware, racks, PDUs, switches, OS and virtualisation licences, maintenance.

💾
Storage costs

Disks, arrays, SAN/Fibre Channel equipment, storage administration.

🌐
Network costs

LAN switches, load balancers, bandwidth, network administration.

👷
IT labour

Server, storage, network and security administrators; support engineers.

🏢
Facilities

Building space, power, cooling, physical security — easy to forget, always present.

🎁
Soft benefits

Developer productivity, agility, global reach — real value, harder to put in RM.

On-premises (Black Friday)

Required: 20 servers Purchased: 100 servers (for peak) Idle most of the year: 80

The company permanently owns peak capacity it rarely needs.

Cloud (Black Friday)

Normal: 20 Black Friday: 100 After: 20

Capacity follows demand — the company is never stuck owning idle servers.

Before you build: the AWS Pricing Calculator

Once CloudMart decides "we might deploy 10 EC2 instances, storage and a database," it wants to know approximately what that architecture will cost before creating anything. That's the Pricing Calculator's whole job — estimate monthly cost, model solutions before building them, compare configurations and terms.

Tool/conceptMain question
TCOIs AWS favourable compared with alternatives such as on-premises?
Pricing CalculatorWhat might my proposed AWS architecture cost?

Exam lens

  • The Pricing Calculator predicts from your assumptions; the bill charges from reality. An estimate of $120/month does not guarantee an invoice of exactly $120 — real usage (more instances, more data transferred, something left running) can differ.
  • TCO is not a universal law that AWS is always cheaper — a slide showing a 96% saving is one illustrative example, not a guarantee. The real lesson: calculate all costs, compare the specific alternatives, then decide.
  • TCO can include non-cost business benefits too: resource optimisation, security/compliance, disaster recovery, faster provisioning, continuous cost optimisation — not just "which number is smaller."
  • Hard benefits are directly measurable financial savings; soft benefits (agility, productivity, reach) are real but not easily priced.
SCENARIO

"Should we close our physical data centre and move to AWS?"

Total Cost of Ownership analysis. Compares hardware, storage, network, facilities, labour and maintenance against AWS as a whole.
SCENARIO

"We have not built the application yet and want to estimate its monthly EC2 and storage cost."

AWS Pricing Calculator — a different tool, covered next lesson. TCO compares whole worlds; the Calculator estimates one proposed AWS architecture.

Quick check

A comparison says "AWS compute = RM15,000, physical server = RM20,000, so AWS saves RM5,000." What's missing?

Almost everything else. The physical server also needs networking, storage, software licences, administrators, building space, power, cooling and maintenance — pretending those are free makes for wonderfully optimistic accounting. TCO exists specifically to capture them.
MODULE 2 · GUIDED LESSON 3 OF 5

🏛️ AWS Organizations: The Head Office

CloudMart grows and now has Production, Development, Testing, Finance, HR, Security and Research. Putting everything into one AWS account becomes messy — so who manages all these accounts?

HEAD OFFICE AND BRANCHES

AWS Organizations centrally manages multiple AWS accounts

Think of AWS Organizations as the company's head office and individual AWS accounts as its branches. It offers policy-based account management, group-based account management, APIs for automation, and consolidated billing.

University analogy

A rule applied to the Engineering Faculty affects the departments under it. AWS Organizations uses the same hierarchy.

Organization ↓ Root ↓ Organizational Units (OUs) ↓ AWS accounts CloudMart Organization ├── Production OU │ ├── Website account │ └── Database account └── Development OU ├── Dev account └── Test account

Organizational Units (OUs)

A logical group of AWS accounts.

Policies can be applied to a whole OU rather than manually treating every account independently — the same rule cascades down to every account inside it.

Consolidated billing

One central billing view across every member account.

Without it: Account A, B, C, D each get separate bills. With AWS Organizations: all of them roll up into one consolidated view — total company spend, cost by account, cost by department.

Service Control Policies (SCPs)

Organisation-level permission ceilings — they limit maximum permissions, they don't grant any.

An SCP is the fence around the property; IAM decides which doors a specific employee can open. If an SCP permits S3, that does not mean every user automatically gets S3 access — IAM must still grant it. Effective access = allowed by the SCP boundary AND allowed by IAM.

Exam lens

  • AWS Organizations = accounts. IAM = identities. "Centrally manage 30 AWS accounts" → Organizations. "Control what a developer can do inside an account" → IAM. They work together but solve different layers.
  • Organizations does not replace IAM — don't write that it does.
  • Organizations can be accessed through the Management Console, CLI, SDKs and the HTTPS Query API — manually or programmatically.
SCENARIO

A company has 40 AWS accounts and wants centralized management and consolidated billing.

AWS Organizations. "Multiple accounts," "centralized" and "consolidated billing" are practically a neon sign.
SCENARIO

The organisation wants to control what an individual developer can do inside one account.

IAM. That's identity-level permission, not account-level management.

Quick check

An SCP allows the Production OU to use S3. Does every user in every account under that OU now have S3 access?

No. The SCP only sets the ceiling — it removes the organisation-level block on S3. Each individual user still needs IAM to actually grant them S3 permissions. Effective access requires both the SCP boundary and IAM to agree.
MODULE 2 · GUIDED LESSON 4 OF 5

📊 Billing & Cost Management Tools

Once CloudMart is actually running on AWS, the question changes from "what might this cost?" to "what are we actually spending?" Five distinct tools answer five distinct questions.

THE HOUSEHOLD ANALOGY

Five tools, five different jobs

AWS provides several distinct billing tools because these are genuinely distinct questions — a quick overview is not the same job as itemised charges, which is not the same job as trend analysis, which is not the same job as a spending alert, which is not the same job as a detailed export.

AWS toolHousehold analogyThink
Billing DashboardQuick financial overviewOverview
AWS BillsItemised utility billCharges
Cost ExplorerGraphs showing spending patternsAnalyse
AWS BudgetsMonthly spending limit and warningThreshold / alert
Cost and Usage ReportDetailed transaction-level spreadsheetDetailed data

AWS Billing Dashboard

"What is happening with my AWS spending?" — a central overview, not raw detail.

Shows a spend summary, month-to-date spending by service, and a forecast at a glance.

AWS Bills

"What was I charged for?" Inspect the charges that make up the bill.

Like an electricity invoice: the total says RM300, and Bills shows where that RM300 came from — by service, Region and usage.

AWS Cost Explorer

Analyse and visualise cost and usage patterns over time.

The bill says "you spent $500." Cost Explorer says how that spending changed over time and where it came from — why did costs increase, which service costs the most, how does this month compare?

AWS Budgets

"Warn me when spending approaches my limit." Set a target, get notified.

Set a monthly target (e.g. $1,000) and a warning threshold; when spend approaches it, a notification/action workflow triggers. It monitors — it does not enforce a hard cap.

Cost and Usage Report

Detailed, line-item cost and usage data — product code, usage type, AZ, amount, currency.

Where the Billing Dashboard is the executive summary, the CUR is what an accountant or data team wants for deep analysis or feeding into their own reporting system.

Exam lens

  • Pricing Calculator (before) vs Cost Explorer (after/during). Calculator estimates a planned architecture; Explorer analyses spending that already happened. Don't swap them.
  • Cost Explorer (investigate) vs Budgets (alert against a target). Explorer asks "what happened?"; Budgets asks "are we within target?"
  • A budget is not a force field around the credit card — if resources keep running, they keep incurring charges. Budgets is a monitoring and alerting mechanism, not a hard spending cap.
SCENARIO

"Finance wants to know why AWS expenditure increased over the last several months."

AWS Cost Explorer. Analysing a historical cost trend.
SCENARIO

"Management wants an alert when spending approaches the company's monthly target."

AWS Budgets. Target + warning threshold.
SCENARIO

"The finance team wants highly detailed AWS usage and cost data for its own reporting system."

AWS Cost and Usage Report. Detailed, line-item export for external analysis.

Quick check

A manager asks "how much did EC2 cost us this month?" Which tool answers this fastest — Bills or the Cost and Usage Report?

Bills. It gives a human-readable breakdown of charges by service — exactly what a manager needs. The Cost and Usage Report is for a finance-data team building its own detailed analytical system, not a quick manager-level question.
MODULE 2 · GUIDED LESSON 5 OF 5

🛟 AWS Support Plans

A student experimenting with AWS does not need the same support relationship as a bank running mission-critical payment systems. AWS provides four support plans, scaled to business impact.

SUPPORT IS ABOUT BUSINESS IMPACT

The more severe the consequences of failure, the stronger the support

Experiment / ordinary access → Basic. Early development → Developer. Production → Business. Mission-critical → Enterprise. That single ladder explains all four plans without memorising four separate definitions.

📘
Basic

General support resources: Resource Center, Service Health Dashboard, FAQs, forums, health checks.

🧪
Developer

Early development on AWS — a small team building/testing its first application.

🏢
Business

Production workloads — a live ecommerce site where real customers depend on it.

🚨
Enterprise

Business- and mission-critical workloads — a core banking or payment system.

The severity ladder

Do not memorise exact response-time numbers unless your lecturer specifically requires the table — those are commercial terms that change over time. Know the ladder instead.

Experiment / ordinary access → Basic Early development → Developer Production → Business Mission-critical → Enterprise Minor issue → lower urgency Production impaired → higher urgency Business-critical system down → highest urgency

The support trio — easy to mix up

AWS support featureThink
Technical Account Manager (TAM)Proactive technical guidance
AWS Trusted AdvisorBest-practice recommendations
AWS Support ConciergeAccount assistance

Trusted Advisor is an AWS service — a "consultant robot" examining your environment, not a human engineer. The module's own sample question: which service provides infrastructure security optimisation recommendations? Answer: AWS Trusted Advisor.

Exam lens

  • Enterprise Support ≠ "most expensive, therefore always best." It's positioned specifically for business- and mission-critical workloads, not premium bragging rights.
  • TAM ≠ account-billing assistant — that's Support Concierge's job. TAM is proactive technical guidance.
  • Trusted Advisor is not a human support engineer; it's an automated recommendations service.
SCENARIO

A developer is building an early-stage application and needs additional technical support.

Developer Support.
SCENARIO

A company's mission-critical system requires the strongest support relationship shown in the module.

Enterprise Support.
SCENARIO

An organisation wants proactive technical guidance from AWS.

Technical Account Manager (TAM).

Quick check

A company wants AWS to flag potential security and cost-optimisation issues in its existing environment. Which feature — TAM, Trusted Advisor, or Support Concierge?

Trusted Advisor. It examines your environment and surfaces best-practice recommendations ("this could be improved," "this configuration has a potential issue") — exactly the module's own sample question about security optimisation recommendations.
